title: Knowledge Check 2 - Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 - OmniStudio Fundamentals. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A pricing lookup is used by three different flows in a client's org. How should the architect approach this capability?
options: Build a separate copy of the lookup inside each flow.
Build it once as a reusable Integration Procedure and invoke it from each flow.
Build it as a FlexCard on each page.
Skip the lookup and hardcode the pricing.
questions.explanation: A capability used by many flows belongs in a reusable Integration Procedure so it is built once and invoked everywhere, which reduces duplication and maintenance. Option A is wrong because duplicating the lookup in each flow is exactly the maintenance problem to avoid. Option C is wrong because a FlexCard displays data rather than orchestrating a reusable system call. Option D is wrong because hardcoding pricing is not a real solution.

questions.question: A consultant must maintain a client's OmniStudio artifacts, and the team has no Apex developers. Which consideration should most influence the tool choice?
options: Prefer declarative tools such as OmniScripts and Data Mappers that a consultant can maintain, over custom Apex.
Prefer custom Apex because it is more flexible.
Choose tools based only on the customer's favorite.
Avoid OmniStudio and build everything in Apex.
questions.explanation: Maintainability is part of the tool choice, so when a consultant must maintain the artifacts, the architect should prefer declarative tools such as OmniScripts and Data Mappers over custom Apex. Option B is wrong because custom Apex is not maintainable by a consultant-only team. Option C is wrong because the customer's favorite is not a technical driver. Option D is wrong because it abandons the declarative value of OmniStudio.

questions.question: An architect has selected a tool for a requirement, but the tool cannot satisfy the acceptance criteria in the requirements baseline. What should the architect do?
options: Force the tool to fit anyway and proceed.
Re-evaluate the tool choice against the baseline and select one that satisfies the criteria.
Change the acceptance criteria to match the tool.
Skip the requirement entirely.
questions.explanation: The selected tool must satisfy the acceptance criteria, data inputs and outputs, and constraints, so if it cannot, the architect re-evaluates the choice rather than forcing the fit. Option A is wrong because forcing a tool that cannot meet the criteria produces a failed design. Option C is wrong because changing the criteria to match the tool hides the problem. Option D is wrong because skipping the requirement does not solve it.

questions.question: An architect is starting an OmniStudio project and needs to plan deployment and upgrades. What should the architect confirm first?
options: Which runtime the target org uses, because it determines the upgrade path and how artifacts are versioned.
The customer's favorite color scheme.
The number of FlexCards the team can build in a week.
Whether the customer has a marketing team.
questions.explanation: The runtime determines the upgrade path and how artifacts are versioned, so the architect must confirm it early because it shapes deployment and upgrade planning. Option B is wrong because color is not a technical driver. Option C is wrong because build rate is not the first concern. Option D is wrong because marketing is irrelevant to the runtime decision.

questions.question: A customer's org uses the managed package runtime for OmniStudio. What does this mean for how the product is received and upgraded?
options: The customer must rebuild OmniStudio from source code.
The toolset and its runtime ship as a managed package and are upgraded through the vendor's package release process.
The customer can never upgrade OmniStudio.
OmniStudio runs only in the browser with no package.
questions.explanation: In the managed package runtime, the toolset and its runtime ship as a managed package and are upgraded through the vendor's package release process, which is how most customers receive the product. Option A is wrong because customers do not rebuild from source. Option C is wrong because managed packages are upgradable. Option D is wrong because the managed package is installed in the org, not only in the browser.

questions.question: An architect discovers the target org uses the standard runtime rather than the managed package runtime. Why does this matter to the project?
options: It does not matter; the tools behave identically in every way.
It changes how upgrades and versioning are handled, so the architect must plan accordingly.
It means OmniStudio cannot be used at all.
It means the customer needs no license.
questions.explanation: The standard runtime changes how upgrades and versioning are handled, so the architect must plan accordingly rather than assuming the managed package model. Option A is wrong because the runtimes differ in upgrade and versioning behavior. Option C is wrong because the standard runtime still supports OmniStudio. Option D is wrong because licensing is separate from the runtime choice.

questions.question: A customer has strict change control and several customizations that could break on a new OmniStudio version. Which upgrade approach is most appropriate?
options: Automatic upgrades, because they are easiest.
Manual intervention upgrades, so the org controls when and how a new version lands and can test first.
No upgrades ever.
Upgrade only when the customer remembers to.
questions.explanation: An org with strict change control and fragile customizations should use manual intervention upgrades so it controls when and how a new version lands and can test in a sandbox first. Option A is wrong because automatic upgrades could land a breaking change without review. Option C is wrong because never upgrading blocks new features and fixes. Option D is wrong because upgrades should be planned, not remembered.

questions.question: An architect is choosing between automatic and manual upgrades for a low-risk org with no fragile customizations. What is the main benefit of automatic upgrades in this case?
options: They keep the org current with minimal effort.
They guarantee no behavior changes.
They remove the need for a license.
They prevent all bugs.
questions.explanation: Automatic upgrades keep the org current with minimal effort, which is the right fit for a low-risk org that can accept the new version's behavior without review. Option B is wrong because a new version can still change behavior. Option C is wrong because licensing is separate from the upgrade path. Option D is wrong because no upgrade prevents all bugs.

questions.question: A team plans a manual intervention upgrade. What is the correct sequence before the production upgrade?
options: Upgrade production immediately and review afterward.
Review the release notes, test the new version in a sandbox against the org's artifacts, then schedule the production upgrade at a controlled time.
Skip testing because the new version is always safe.
Upgrade production and production only, with no sandbox.
questions.explanation: A manual intervention upgrade follows a controlled sequence: review the release notes, test the new version in a sandbox against the org's artifacts, then schedule the production upgrade at a controlled time. Option A is wrong because upgrading production before review risks breaking artifacts. Option C is wrong because new versions are not always safe. Option D is wrong because sandbox testing is a required step.

questions.question: A user has been assigned an OmniStudio Permission Set but still cannot use the OmniStudio features. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: The user needs a Permission Set License, which grants the right to use the licensed feature, in addition to the Permission Set.
The user needs a new laptop.
The user needs to be an admin.
The user needs to restart the browser.
questions.explanation: The Permission Set License grants the right to use the licensed feature, while the Permission Set grants the actual access, and both are typically required, so a user with only the Permission Set is missing the license. Option B is wrong because hardware is not the issue. Option C is wrong because admin rights are not the missing license. Option D is wrong because a browser restart does not grant a license.

questions.question: An architect is planning which users get OmniStudio access. What is the correct approach to licensing?
options: Assign the Permission Set License and Permission Set only to the users who actually need OmniStudio features.
Assign every user in the org both the license and the permission set.
Assign no licenses and rely on the base platform.
Assign only the Permission Set License to everyone.
questions.explanation: The architect should assign the Permission Set License and Permission Set only to users who actually need OmniStudio features, because over-licensing costs money and under-licensing blocks users. Option B is wrong because licensing everyone wastes money. Option C is wrong because OmniStudio is a licensed product that needs the license. Option D is wrong because the Permission Set is also required for actual access.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Permission Set License and a Permission Set in OmniStudio?
options: They are the same thing with two names.
The Permission Set License determines whether a user is entitled to the feature, while the Permission Set determines what the user can actually do with it.
The Permission Set grants the license automatically.
The Permission Set License is only for admins.
questions.explanation: The Permission Set License determines whether a user is entitled to the licensed feature, while the Permission Set determines what the user can actually do with it, and both are typically required. Option A is wrong because they are distinct layers. Option C is wrong because a Permission Set does not grant the license. Option D is wrong because the Permission Set License is not admin-only.

questions.question: A client has three roles that need OmniStudio: builders, reviewers, and end users. How should the architect grant access?
options: Give every user the full builder permission set and license.
Create a small set of role-based permission sets, such as builder, reviewer, and end user, assign each the minimum access it needs, and assign the appropriate license to each role's users.
Create a separate permission set for every individual user.
Give no one any access and rely on the base platform.
questions.explanation: The architect should create a small set of role-based permission sets, assign each the minimum access it needs, and assign the appropriate Permission Set License to each role's users, which is maintainable and least-privilege. Option A is wrong because giving everyone the full builder set over-grants access. Option C is wrong because one-off sets per person are unmaintainable. Option D is wrong because OmniStudio needs the license and permission sets to be usable.

questions.question: An end user only needs to run an OmniScript, not create artifacts. What is the correct access to grant?
options: The full builder permission set and license.
A permission set that allows running the OmniScript, with the appropriate Permission Set License, and nothing more.
Admin access to the whole org.
No permission set, only the license.
questions.explanation: The architect should grant the minimum access each role needs, so an end user gets a permission set that allows running the OmniScript plus the appropriate Permission Set License, and nothing more. Option A is wrong because the full builder set over-grants. Option C is wrong because admin access is far more than needed. Option D is wrong because the user needs the Permission Set for actual access, not just the license.

questions.question: A user who held an OmniStudio Permission Set License has left the company. What should the architect or admin do?
options: Leave the license and permission set assigned.
Adjust the user's license and permission set as part of offboarding, and review the org's license and permission set assignments periodically.
Assign the license to a random remaining user.
Delete the license from the org entirely.
questions.explanation: Because Permission Set Licenses are a costed entitlement, the architect or admin should adjust a departing user's license and permission set as part of offboarding and review assignments periodically. Option A is wrong because leaving it assigned wastes a costed license. Option C is wrong because assigning to a random user is not a plan. Option D is wrong because deleting the license from the org removes it for everyone who needs it.
